cells.tense: There's a shape in the mess now, and you can say how you found it.
cells.act: start something for the spark of starting
cells.ask: Begin something you have no way to finish yet — a page, a sketch, a first attempt. Keep it off the plan. The same quick read, with the aim taken off.
cells.core:
What you do with a mess is find the line through it — the real one, not the tidy one — and then put up the shape that lets other people walk through. That's what's working here. The reasoning is quick and it's aimed at something true. The structure holds after you leave, and it holds when someone else takes it over.

What hasn't had room is starting for no reason. Begin something small with nothing waiting on it — a first attempt, a page nobody will see. A week of that, and the structures you hold stay useful instead of airtight. Setting a pattern and standing inside one are different things, and the week will show you which one you're doing.
cells.sheetLine: You set shapes other people can walk through.
cells.verb: cutting through to what's actually true, fast
cells.place: where the pattern gets set and the structure goes up

cells.tense: You're bracing for something that hasn't arrived, and firing first anyway.
cells.act: cut through the inertia with one decisive act
cells.ask: Take one decision that's been sitting — real, small, almost made. Make it once today and add nothing after it. Let the week run on the decision.
cells.core:
The reasoning has gotten so fast it's arriving before the situation does. Plans get rebuilt for a week that hasn't happened, and the structure keeps shifting under the people standing on it. That's the tell: the thinking outruns the ground, and you're braced for something nobody has said yet.

One clean move brings it back. Choose something that's been undecided and decide it, once, today. Don't refine it. You'll feel the pull to add a caveat within the hour; let the pull pass. A decision that lands whole gives the pattern something solid to sit on. A day goes by and the plan is still the plan — anything that truly needs changing can be changed next week, alongside the people it touches.

cells.tense: You stood at the door a long time, and it hasn't moved since.
cells.act: teach what you feel by doing it with others
cells.ask: Pick a task, a game, a route you've done many times. Walk somebody through it while you do it, and let their pace set the speed. An afternoon, no more.
cells.core:
The door that was yours to walk through is behind you now, and the pen's still down. There's no shape on the page, and you're not sure your hand is the one that should hold it. The clear thinking is there somewhere; it just isn't landing. You can see the tool and not the task.

What puts charge back into the line isn't effort aimed at the blank page. Do something beside another person. Take a task your hands have repeated enough times that they know it, and do it in front of somebody — no structure to defend yet, letting them watch how you hold it when it goes sideways. Structure comes back from the inside, not from the plan. The pattern lives in the hands, and the hands move when somebody is across from them.
cells.sheetLine: The door is behind you. The page is still blank.

cells.tense: You're already writing this, and you don't call the pen yours.
cells.act: hold space for what someone feels without fixing it
cells.ask: When someone brings you something, sit with it for one exchange before you reach for the fix — one plain question, then stay in their answer.
cells.core:
The structure around you and the careful thinking behind it are mostly yours, and when somebody names it you credit the situation. That isn't modesty. It's a hand that has been drawing lines so long the lines look like they were already there.

Sit with what a person is carrying before you reach for the shape of it. Not a technique to add — a pause where the pattern gets noticed instead of assembled. The faster your read is, the more it looks like the world rather than like you, and that's the cost of the speed. Put your name on it where only you can hear it. No announcement, just the true account. It's yours, and you're allowed to know it quietly.

attempts.check: Unsupported claim: 'things make sense in your presence' — I can't say how anyone else experiences them, so that stays out. Reader's likely objection: 'I'm not anxious, I just think faster than everyone here' — so the Too Much cell describes the tempo and the pre-writing of what hasn't happened, not a diagnosis. The Balanced ask (start something with no destination, inside the rules) still teaches something if the read is wrong, and it's useful to anyone who already drafts before they move; the sentence that serves the writer is 'You're already drafting the next version of it,' which is a flourish I cut. The Too Much ask is the one I'd defend least if the reader says nothing's rushed — it still leaves them a week of their own material.
